summary: For ages 9-11, teach insect anatomy as structure-serves-function: compound eyes (arrays of many tiny lenses), spiracles (breathing holes along the body), diet-specialised mouthparts (chewing mandibles in beetles, coiled sucking proboscis in butterflies, sponging pad in flies), moulting the rigid exoskeleton to grow, and biomimicry (engineers copying insect designs). Each specialised part should be explained by the job it does, with strongly magnified imagery so tiny structures are visible. The anchoring puzzle is: if your skeleton is on the OUTSIDE, how do you grow? — answered by moulting.
misconceptions: 'Insects breathe through their mouth/nose' — they breathe via spiracles and tracheae along the body.
'Compound eyes work like our single-lens eyes' — they are arrays of many tiny lenses.
'All insects eat the same way' — mouthparts are specialised to diet.
'Insects grow continuously like us' — growth is stepwise, requiring moulting of the rigid exoskeleton.
'The exoskeleton grows with the insect' — it doesn't; it must be shed and replaced.

activities.title: Explore a magnified insect: each part and the job it does
steps: Study a strongly magnified, highly detailed insect image so tiny structures (lenses, spiracles) are actually visible.

Examine the bulging eye, zoomed in until its surface resolves into many tiny hexagonal lenses (thousands in insects such as flies and dragonflies); compare a mosaic 'insect-vision' view of the world and describe why many lenses pointing in different directions help spot movement quickly across a wide view, even though the picture is less sharp than ours.
Examine the mouth across a beetle (crunching mandibles), a butterfly (coiled drinking-straw proboscis) and a fly (sponging pad); for each, pair it with the food it is built for.
Find the small spiracles dotted along the body and state that air enters there, along the body, not through the mouth.
Confront the puzzle posed by the shell: 'if your skeleton is on the OUTSIDE, how do you grow?' then view a moult sequence of the insect wriggling out of its old casing.
For each structure, state in one sentence the job it does before moving on.
activities.insight: Each specialised insect structure exists because of the job it does: mouthparts match diet, spiracles enable breathing under a rigid exoskeleton, and compound eyes are arrays of many lenses — not single-lens eyes like ours.

activities.title: Match the mouthpart to its food, and moult to grow
steps: Match each mouthpart to the food it is built for: proboscis → nectar, mandibles → leaf, sponging pad → spilled liquid.
Explain why the match works using tool analogies: a coiled straw can suck but cannot cut; jaws can cut but cannot reach deep into a flower.
Reason about a constraint: could an adult butterfly eat a leaf the way a beetle does? Explain why not.

Trigger a moult sequence as the insect outgrows its shell, and explain that the insect's outer size increases in steps because the hard exoskeleton cannot stretch much and must be shed and replaced — the new, soft exoskeleton expands before it hardens; the old one does not grow with the insect.
activities.insight: Form constrains what an animal can do: mouthparts are not interchangeable, and a rigid exoskeleton forces stepwise growth by moulting.

activities.title: Infer function from an unfamiliar structure, and explore biomimicry
steps: Given a new structure not studied directly (for example a mosquito's or aphid's needle-like piercing-sucking mouthparts), infer the kind of food the insect eats and explain the reasoning.

Give one example of biomimicry where human technology is inspired by an insect structure or ability, pairing the structure with the design (for example compound eye → camera array; exoskeleton → body armour or robotics).
Pick one insect structure and propose what it might inspire in engineering or design, explaining the shared function.
activities.insight: Structure-function reasoning transfers: you can predict an insect's diet from an unfamiliar mouthpart, and the same principle explains why engineers copy insect designs.

checkQuestion: A beetle has strong jaws (mandibles) for chewing, while a butterfly has a long thin coiled tube (a proboscis) instead. Why do these two insects have such different mouthparts? And here's a puzzle: a butterfly drinks nectar from deep inside flowers — could it eat a leaf the way a beetle does? Explain.
checkAnswer: Their mouthparts differ because they eat different foods, and each mouthpart suits its food. The beetle chews solid food (leaves, other insects) so it needs hard jaws. The butterfly drinks liquid nectar from deep in flowers, so it needs a long thin tube to reach and suck it up — it can't chew. A butterfly could NOT eat a leaf like a beetle: its proboscis is a drinking straw, not a cutting tool, so it can only take liquids. Structure matches function.
